utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Mathias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President, good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Mirna Milanovic, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else present in the courtroom. The Trial Chamber is very happy to see the model that disappeared for a few weeks. We have it before us again now. And this should facilitate the task of following the witnesses when it's necessary to find the locations of routes, villages, or other sites. We'll now continue with -- we'll now commence with the cross-examination of the witness, unless Defence counsel has anything to say. Yes, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're in open session, I'll address the issue of tendering the documents contained in the binder after the witness has been heard. You have numbered them. The first one is 511, the second one 603 and so on. For reasons that have to do with copying documents, the Registrar would like to all the numbers of the original - 511, 603, et cetera - all these numbers marked for identification. On the first list we would have a number for the document marked for identification. And after the witness has been heard, you can -- after the witness has identified the documents, we could then give these exhibits definitive numbers. They would no longer be marked for identification. Is this in any way problematic for you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That would make matters easier for the Defence counsel. The entire list that we provided -- the entire list of documents could be marked for identification, and once some of the exhibits we showed to the witness admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber, at that stage we could delete the number used for identification and use the same number that was previously indicated on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, as far as this issue is concerned, we will have a number for the document which will be marked for identification. We will then delete this number used for identification once the witness has identified the relevant document. No comments, no observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar has told me that Defence counsel should also provide an official list of the documents with relevant numbers, and then you will ask us, after the witness's examination, for us to delete the numbers used for identification and for the exhibits to be given definitive numbers. This will be done provided that the documents have been identified and haven't been contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would like to make sure that you are receiving interpretation. If so, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. My name is Daryl Mundis. I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case. I'm going to be asking you some questions this afternoon, sir. And it's certainly not my intention in any way to confuse you, so if any of my questions are not clear, I would simply ask you to say so, or if you don't understand a question, to say so and I will either repeat or rephrase the question. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, please, the precise dates that you were the commanding officer of the 312th.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the 312th Motorised Brigade, I acted as commander from mid-November. Now, why am I not stating the exact date? It is because of the fact that the period during which the brigade was established was largely spent on various issues involving the establishment of the staff. They worked together with the Territorial Defence. So that the official date of the establishment of the 312th Motorised Brigade and my first report in my capacity of brigade commander goes back to the 25th November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for how long did you remain in that position as commander of the 312th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained in that position until the 26th of April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, during the period from the 25th of November 1992 until the end of 1993, where were the headquarters of the 312th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters of the 312th Motorised Brigade at the very beginning was located in Travnik, more specifically in the facilities that had been requisitioned from the former company which was called either Sebisic or something to that effect. But I know that it was a former construction company, whose premises were in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And sir, you said from -- or at the very beginning, it was located there. Did your headquarters remain in that building throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But let me just tell you that after the units had been established, and after the initial period of the work of the brigade staff passed, the headquarters of the brigade also worked from a forward command post which was located in the vicinity of the front line of the Serb forces in the village of Turici which is located to the west of Travnik, some 6 kilometres away from the town. The village of Turici is a Muslim village, and that is where the forward command post was located. However, the main command post, the headquarters was still in Travnik town. And the next thing that might be of interest to you is the fact that the brigade command, after the fighting began and when the Croat population from the villages located to the left of the road - rather, to the south of the main road, that is, Travnik-Jajce main road, when we took possession of all of those abandoned Croat villages in order to provide security and prevent plunder, so it was with that objective in mind that the command in Travnik, the oldest operations group, it was ordered that parts of the brigade be located or transferred to the village of Kraljevica. This was one of the villages that had been abandoned by their Croat population with the exception of just a few families that remained in that village. That date must have been sometime around the 15th of June 1993. As of that date, the command had its seat, its headquarters in the village of Kraljevica. I don't know whether this is enough in terms of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine, sir, thank you. Now, from the period of the -- from the mid-November 1992 through the end of 1993, can you tell us, chronologically, from the beginning of when you assumed command to the end of 1993, to whom you reported directly. Who was your immediate supervisor? And if that changed throughout that period, if you could indicate that, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning when the 312th Motorised Brigade was established, in light of the command and control system of our superior command, the command of the 3rd Corps, we received tasks -- or rather, we were tasked with the duty to report to the -- to that command about all measures and all assignments that we had and about which we had to inform our superior command. That activity was carried out in a similar manner as it is normally done in every other modern army. We had weekly reports and monthly reports. Later, because of a large number of units and the very complicated communication lines that the headquarters had with their front lines, and also because of the fact that there were several brigade commands, operations units were established in order to unite in a given area several brigades. In Bugojno, for instance, the Operations Group West was established, and the 312th Motorised Brigade became part of that operations group. It was sometime in either March or April that I received a task -- or rather, I was ordered to send my reports to the West Operations Group. There's another thing that might be of interest to you: At the same time, in the same month when the West Operations Group was established, the operations group called Bosanska Krajina was established in Travnik. Our brigades, the Travnik brigades, the 312th and 306th brigades were not part of that operations group because we were under the West Operations Group. But I know, for instance, that the 17th Brigade came under this Bosanska Krajina Operations Group. So the reporting system was quite difficult, and it is very complicated to get in touch with Operations Group West, and that is why we sent our reports to both of these operations group, both to the West Operations Group and the Bosanska Krajina operations Group during the period of time you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if I understand you correctly, at the beginning, you reported directly to the 3rd Corps commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then sometime in the spring of 1993 when the Operation Group West was formed, you reported to the commander of that operational group?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time the Operation Group West was formed, can you tell us who was the commander of that operational group.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Operation Group West from the day it was established until the end was Brigadier Selmo Cikotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, sir, at no point in time was the 312th Motorised Brigade part of Operation Group Bosanska Krajina. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, for the record, because we have a number of documents as well, can you please spell for the Trial Chamber the Bosnian word for "west."

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Z-a-p-a-d.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So if we have documents that refer to Operational Group Zapad, that would be Operational Group West?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, at the time OG Zapad was formed, what other brigades were part of that operational group?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not precise enough, I apologise for the Chamber in advance. I was not duty-bound to know exactly which brigades, but I know that the following came under that group: 306th, 312th, 317th, 307th. I don't know whether I mentioned 308th Brigade. Those were the units which were part of OG West.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the period 1993, did the 312th Motorised Brigade have a specific area of responsibility, a geographic area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, the 312th Motorised Brigade took over the fighting area that they inherited from the territorial staff. I showed this yesterday. It was west of Travnik in the area of Turbe battleground. And also to the left and the south of Turbe, a number of villages there, and also an area which extended to the north of Turbe. It was a classical military front line. This was -- this had been the area of responsibility of the Territorial Defence. But this area became area of responsibility of the 312th Motorised Brigade, and all elements which are part of the brigade, including logistics and elements of the logistics as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I know you made a number of indications yesterday on a large colour map that was here in the courtroom. I would ask you if you could, please, to perhaps with the assistance of the usher, if you could take one of the markers, and on the map behind you make a few markings for me as I ask you to do so. You told us yesterday about front lines between the 312th and the Bosnian Serb forces or the VRS or what later became known as the VRS. Can you please mark the front -- let me ask you this first: The front line in that area, did it move a lot during 1993, the front line between your forces and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let me see if I got this right, whether the front line between us and VRS moved in 1993. Let me think: In 1993, no. Sorry, I was confused a bit because I was thinking of 1992 when the situation was much more favourable to the then TO staff. I can give you more information on that if you want. As for 1993, that was your question: The area was the same as I described it yesterday. I can maybe indicate a number of facilities, or rather villages which were part of this area to make things clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you so that we don't end up with a map with too much information on it, if you could just draw the front line between the 312th and the VRS during 1993. If you could mark that on the map for me, if you see it on the map, the area.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Turbe is here. I'm going to indicate the locations with respect to areas. Secevo, the village of Secevo, for instance. Shall I make a circle or underline it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could visually mark where the line went, as one might see on an operational map in a military room.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we please make sure the witness's mic is on. We can hardly hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this would roughly be the line in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if you could then, to the northwest of that line, if you could write the initials "VRS" for where the Serb forces were.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then perhaps to the southeast or to the south or to the right-hand side of that line indicate where the 312th was, perhaps by just writing the numbers "312."

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few more questions about the map. Maybe we'll just deal with them all now. At some point in 1993, was the 312th Brigade also maintaining a front line against the Croat or HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993? You mean -- you don't have any specific period in mind, just in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During 1993. Did the 312th Motorised Brigade undergo any kind of combat or have a front line that they were opposed to the Bosnian Croat or HVO forces? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see now. There was some activity in the latter half of June and later in the second half of that year. Those events caused the 312th Brigade, in addition to a number of troops that secured that area against incursions of the VRS, caused the brigade to undergo a number of clashes with HVO at the time. I had a number of troops on leave for a while, and they entered, those forces entered -- if you understand me correctly, the Territorial Defence staff at that time had their geographically deployed units, the units that were connected to particular facilities, particular streets or neighbourhoods in that area. And that is how this geographical area unit was located, specifically in the territory of the Slimene local commune. Because this is where those incidents started, the incidents which then developed into a conflict with HVO. My troops were on leave at the time, and they came under the command of those area units, and they made themselves available for the Defence against HVO units. And that is how as early as 1993 we had a front line against HVO in the area of Slimene. I am referring mainly to the regional road between Travnik and Novi Travnik, in the area of Slimene. And right before Slimene is where the Defence line of the 312th Brigade was located. Do you want me to indicate that on the map as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could, if it's possible on the map, if you can indicate the line between the 312th and the HVO forces in the area that you've just indicated.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would roughly be the line, if you're talking about the 312th. The 306th was to the left, or rather to the north, and southwest we had the 308th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could, if you could indicate where those two units were that you just mentioned, the 308th... ?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want me to write down the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact location of the lines. I'll just write down the. Let me also indicate here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, if you could, please, sir, to the southeast of that line you've just drawn indicate again on the map that that was the HVO, that on the line -- that on the opposite side of that line that you just drew were the HVO forces. If you could just mark that for us.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm able to be precise. But it was right across the road to Novi Travnik. I shall mark it with a dotted line because of a certain degree of imprecision, because I cannot remember the exact location at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. And if you could then, to the right-hand side and below the dotted line, simply indicate "HVO" so we can all remember several weeks from now what it is that you've drawn.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before we finish with the map, perhaps if you could in the right-hand corner down towards the bottom where there's some white space, if you could just initial that or sign your name on this map and put today's date, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here? [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, one last question about the map: The two lines that you've drawn, the two solid lines, would it be fair to say that the 312th Brigade, that its area was within those two lines?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Militarily speaking, the area of responsibility involves everything there is -- that's there. As for battleground and operations theatre, it had to do with the deployment -- the military or combat deployment of armed troops and everything that was indicated in area, in that terrain. As for the area of responsibility, I could have marked where the 17th was, where the battalion of the 7th was, and the reserve police force. There were a number of various elements there. There was a command of the oldest operational group there as well. So when talking about area of responsibility, it has to do with the actual deployment of troops, armed troops facing the enemy lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that -- thank you for correcting me on that. Let me ask you a couple of questions, then, in terms of following up on what you just told us. You mentioned that there was a unit of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade that was in the area that you've just pointed to.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was the battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. I mean, I merely indicated the area of the 312th. Now, if you're referring to specific positions, I don't know that. Are you asking me about the actual position of the 7th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's break this down into a couple of smaller questions. You mentioned the battalion of the 7th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know which battalion of the 7th was in this area?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion, I assume. The reason why I can only assume is because I did not always have opportunity to work with those guys from the brigade command, and their headquarters were in Zenica. You know that it is brigade commands that operate at the same level. They had their own communication line with Zenica. But yes, we were more or less informed about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Because, of course, you need to know if there were friendly forces in the area where your troops were operating so as to avoid any blue-on-blue or red-on-red fatalities?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. As I indicated, I mean, I described the 7th -- the battalion of the 7th as friendly force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Exactly. Do you know who the commander in 1993 -- the early part of 1993, at least, who the commander of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Brigade was?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I'm really sorry, but I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know -- sir, do you know where the headquarters of the 1st Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was located?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me right, their headquarters were located next to the former building of the Ministry of the Interior, next door, as far as I remember. If we go back a little, I know that members of the HVO hoisted a flag of the State of Croatia on that building which then provoked a number of incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I take it when you say the "Ministry of the Interior building," you're referring to the MUP building in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Travnik. It's not a very large building. It's a two-storey house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I think we're finished with the map, so if you would like to sit down, that's fine. If you prefer to stand, I don't mind that either, but we're done with the map for now. Thank you. Sir, during the period in 1993, were there any facilities within the area where the 312th was located where soldiers of the 3rd Corps were trained?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean, "where they were trained"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, during 1993 -- let's back up, then. During 1993, did the 312th Motorised Brigade undergo regular military training? Did you train your troops?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if only that had been possible. I do apologise. I understand your question now. We did train the troops, but the training wasn't such that I could train the entire unit, platoons, companies, and battalion. Regardless of the kind of training concerned, the training was partial. It involved individuals, the training of individuals, the training of groups, and men who were in units and were not engaged in combat operations at the time. So our plan was to finish the cycle of training, whether it had to do with introducing them to certain military theories or whether it had to do with the code of conduct, et cetera. Everything that used to be done in peacetime couldn't be done with the brigade members under the conditions that prevailed. But we had such training areas behind the combat lines. I could show you where they Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond were. It was perhaps a kilometre or two behind the lines in an area that wasn't inhabited, and that is where the soldiers were trained in what one would have to do in combat. But we tried to complete the cycle of training regardless of whether it had to do with combat or discipline, et cetera. But the soldiers would be soldiers. There was a man in the unit -- there were men who were shepherds in the unit, and there were others who had university educations. There were some who were quicker and some who were slower. You had to train the establishment units, and sometimes the task was one that took a little time to execute. So the training that was provided was provided in the field, in the combat area, or sometimes in facilities where units were preparing themselves for rotation, preparing to replace men who were already in the field. Such facilities had been requisitioned for the purposes of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, other than these local training areas, if soldiers from your -- from the 312th Motorised Brigade were sent to other areas within the 3rd Corps for training.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That probably did occur. But to be more specific, as far as I can remember, at that time there was a training centre in Zenica, and we had recruits there, too, and we were training recruits there at that time. We were training men who knew nothing about the army, youths who had to do their military service. So this is something that existed at the time. We had this training centre, this educational centre in Zenica, and that is where these men would be trained to become soldiers. And perhaps they were trained in legal matters to a certain extent. Often there were seminars about the security service, and there were issues relating to the assistant commander of the 3rd Corps. He issued instructions, assigned tasks for the forthcoming periods. There were intelligence tasks, et cetera, et cetera. But we had to adapt to the new situation that had developed. The conditions were not such as they had been during peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, who was responsible for this training? Who did the training?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person who was most responsible to the training of brigade members, if we're talking about the training of the entire brigade, was the brigade commander. As far as plans are concerned, engaging a certain part of the brigade, then it's that segment, the battalion commander, that is responsible. If the task was to train men how to carry out certain tasks, train men how to be disciplined, et cetera, then this was his responsibility. But someone from the brigade command had to be present. And this was usually the brigade commander. He had to be present. He had to provide instructions, guidelines, and then after the training had been completed he had to make a closing statement and assign certain tasks after the entire training period had been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of any instance during 1993 when foreign soldiers or foreign fighters or mujahedin conducted any training for members of the 312th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us yesterday that in October or November 1992, General Hadzihasanovic spent some time in Travnik. Other than this occasion, do you remember any instances, other than this time you've told us about, when General Hadzihasanovic visited Travnik or the 312th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just a minute. Yes. Commander Hadzihasanovic visited the brigade. I'll tell you the month. I think it was in June or in August -- in July or August 1993 in my command post in Kraljevica. And the army commander, Mr. Rasim Delic, was there, too. I know that it was a very humid summer day, but I'm not sure whether it was in July or in the August. That was the day when I as a brigade commander received a task from the command of the operations group which was the oldest command. It had been in existence before the command of the 3rd Corps. I was given a task to prepare a briefing which was to be presented to the corps commander and the army commander, and I was to inform them of the preparedness of the brigade, the situation in the brigade, of problems, and I was to make suggestions. The visit occurred in the morning, and he was there for two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than this occasion that you've just told us about, do you recall him being in Travnik or meeting with you or other leaders of the 312th Brigade during 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Knowing Commander Enver, I doubt that he wanted to meet some of my commanders. He wouldn't have wanted to do so without my being presented. But I really can't remember now. If he had been present, I as brigade commander would have been present, too, because he is a soldier just like me and he understands such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than these two occasions when Commander Hadzihasanovic came to Travnik, on how many occasions from the time of your appointment as commander of the 312th to the end of 1993 did you travel to Zenica or anywhere else to meet with General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the brigade had been established, there was a previously assigned task to prepare for a briefing on what had been done with regard to the order for forming a brigade. That was in December 1992. And we informed them of what had been done. We informed them of the level attained, we informed them of the problems, et cetera, et cetera. What I said yesterday -- what I mentioned yesterday were problems that all the brigades had, from Maglaj as far as Gornji Vakuf. Later, I don't remember whether I was there in January, but I know that I went on one other occasion. But the commander wasn't there. His chief, I don't know whether it was Mr. Mekic or someone else, he received us, and afterwards there were certain other events. Information was provided. There were orders, and there was the formation of operation groups. And all our duties, all our tasks, all our reports were forwarded to the operation groups. There was a specific situation in Travnik because we were tied to OG Zapad, and I only saw Mr. Selmo on one occasion, you know, because at the time it was impossible to go there via Donja Vakuf. The Serbian forces were present there. As for the other roads, the checkpoints had already been erected and HVO extremists had already mounted weapons in certain areas, and it was very difficult to pass through. So in the second half of 1993, the situation was very difficult and people were starving. And it's interesting to point out that at that time, the international community was present. There were large numbers of refugees, and the Travnik area is a small area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to a different topic now, sir. Yesterday I believe you told us that your men were occasionally allowed to return to their homes, and that some of them lived in Travnik, Kakanj, and other places in Central Bosnia. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also told us or mentioned, and you were shown some documents to this effect, that a number of soldiers from the 312th Motorised Brigade were referred to competent legal authorities and otherwise disciplined for criminal activity. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also told us that - and this is a quote from the English transcript - "there are quite a lot of proceedings instituted because of looting." And my question, sir, is: First of all, do you recall instituting proceedings concerning looting?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proceedings instituted by the security organs in my brigade, that is to say, by the military police, were then referred to the prosecution office in the municipal court. I no longer remember how they operated because they weren't my subordinates. But I think that at that time, I didn't -- I wasn't much liked by my combatants. You know there was a lot of hunger and people would be sentenced because of stealing a bag of potatoes or they would be sentenced to 60 days in prison. But that was the situation. That's how things were at the time, you know. I understand all the rules. I know what has to be done. But that was the situation and that was what was done. As far as the criminal reports that our brigade service provided to the competent court are concerned, I'm not sure how they proceeded. I'm not sure how they characterised these crimes, because the judicial authorities were after all independent at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just ask you a couple of follow-on questions from this. I guess my question is, sir, you told us you recalled a number of proceedings involving looting. First of all, is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were criminal reports as a result of looting. A number of criminal reports were forwarded to the competent court because of the looting that had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, what geographic area these alleged looting incidents occurred in?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the documents show - and this can be seen in the statement of reasons - it says proceedings were instituted because he stole something from Bosniak houses or Croatian houses or there were villages on the road from -- leading from the position to the house. So it didn't just have to do with abandoned Croatian villages which we really had secured. Let me tell you that my Croatian friends regret not having looted to a greater extent, because after the war they weren't provided with any humanitarian aid or any assistance; although we weren't responsible, because the MUP was present there and the civilian protection and the organs of power. But I did everything that I could to protect all the villages and the Croatian people who had to leave those houses because they were under threat. And thank goodness that people have been able to return and people are happy to be able to live, at least to a certain extent, in their houses, and they don't have to suffer the consequences of what happened during that wartime period in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I am approximately about halfway done with the cross-examination. As Your Honours have probably noted, the witness has given some lengthy and very helpful answers. I would hope I could finish in another 45 or perhaps a little bit longer than that, but not much more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will have a break now, and we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you a series of questions concerning reports or the initiation of investigations into alleged incidents of looting. I understand from what you've told us that some of these locations are not in the area where the 312th was located, but because you told us that your soldiers were occasionally outside of that area, whether on their way home or perhaps doing other things, I'm going to ask you about this nevertheless. I would ask you if you have no information simply to indicate that because there's a lot list of these questions, and we need to move as quickly as possible. Do you recall forwarding any reports or initiating any investigations concerning alleged looting in Dusina in January 1993 by soldiers of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this question falls outside the scope of examination-in-chief. And according to the witness's testimony, he has indicated where his brigade was and where he was present. There are no grounds for asking this witness such a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As far as this issue is concerned, Defence counsel produced an entire series of documents that have to do with soldiers' behaviour, and in particular that have to do with investigations that were launched within the 312th Motorised Brigade. These are documents that were shown to the witness. The Prosecution is asking the witness whether soldiers from the 312th committed acts outside the zone of responsibility of the 312th while they were returning to their families or going away on leave, et cetera. So the question is directly linked to the investigations carried out because it would be reasonable to know whether the soldiers of the 312th committed crimes or misdemeanors that don't fall within the competence of the 312th. So perhaps the witness could answer the question, and perhaps not. Mr. Caber, please answer the question. You have understood it. It's very simple. The Prosecution is asking you whether soldiers from the 312th committed any acts or any crimes that don't fall within your competence; and if you found out about such crimes, what did you do? Because you did launch investigations, et cetera. It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution referred to Dusina, and I didn't have any men in that area, nor did any of my men commit any such acts. They weren't involved in any looting. But I am familiar with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'm going to ask you a series of similar questions about a number of locations, and I will give you the name of the location and the month during the year 1993 when these alleged incidents occurred. Again, do you have any recollection of initiating or forwarding any reports concerning alleged looting in the village of Miletici during April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. There is an error in the translation. It's on page 33, line 17. The last sentence, according to the transcript, is "but I am familiar with these matters," whereas the witness said that he never heard about that, he knew nothing about it, whereas here it says that he knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall initiating any investigations or filing any reports with the competent legal or law enforcement or judicial authorities concerning alleged looting by ABiH soldiers in the village of Miletici during April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the question seems to indicate that the witness already said that he was familiar with these events. I don't think that the Prosecution can ask a question this way. He should first ask whether the witness knows anything about this, and only after having put such a question to the witness can the Prosecution ask whether there were any investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Mundis, in order to be quite clear, it would be best to ask the witness whether he knew anything about looting incidents that didn't fall within his competence for which he was not responsible, and in such a case what did he do. Try and break the question up into two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware of allegations that ABiH soldiers looted civilian property in Miletici during April 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Soldiers from the 312th, not BH soldiers. What's the sense of the question? Because if you're asking about BH soldiers, there were 32.000 of them. He can't be familiar with everything. He's familiar with the soldiers for whom he was responsible. Because let us imagine the following case: A man from the 312th commits an act in another area, and he is arrested. Obviously, this soldiers wouldn't be in the force when he assumes his position, and he might know that something happened [as interpreted]. So you must ask him questions about soldiers under his responsibility. He can't know about soldiers who belonged to the BH in general. Is that what the Defence wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what we wanted to say first of all, and secondly, Mr. President, this question doesn't fall within the scope of the examination-in-chief. And could provisions contained in Rule 90(H) be respected and cross-examination should be limited to examination-in-chief. Going beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief must be justified. Why would the Prosecution want to go beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief? And I think that this is the same principle that was applied to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I'd like to point out to the Defence that in the case of the examination-in-chief, you produced documents about investigations. You showed them to the witness, and there's one document referring to 61 investigations into soldiers from 312th. This is Document Number 959. It's a document which was shown to the witness, and there are 61 cases referred to. On the basis of this document, the Prosecution claims that there is a link, as one says in English. And the Prosecution is asking the witness whether he was aware of any other cases or of cases referred to in the list. Was he aware of any soldiers who had committed crimes outside his zone of responsibility? For example, in an area for which the 306th was responsible or the 17th, for example, or an area for which some other unit was responsible. So Mr. Caber, I think you have understood the question. Do you think you could answer it because at the present a direct link to Document Number 959.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when members of the -- as far as members of the 312th Motorised Brigade are concerned, I cannot be a hundred per cent sure, but I know that my colleagues from other brigades did not inform me of such cases. Therefore, I do not know, and I do not think that members of my units deployed in other areas of responsibility, in areas of responsibility of other brigades, such as 306th, 308th, were not involved in such incidents. And you were right to point out, Your Honour, even members of the 307th, because they were also in the area of Bugojno, people who had come from the villages such as Karaula who had abandoned their places of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Document 959 is concerned, we have 61 cases of looting. We have the names of the perpetrators. We have the references to the Criminal Code. But we do not know the place where these crimes were committed. So the Defence is right. And the Chamber also wanted to ask you this question: As far as these 61 cases are concerned, were these violations committed in the area of Turbe and Travnik where you were deployed, or is it possible that such incidents, such crimes were committed in other areas? That is the question. Is it possible that these incidents took place elsewhere, or is it the case that these crimes were committed only in your area of responsibility? That is, the area of Turbe and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it happened a long time ago. I saw this document only a few days ago. Whether these incidents took place elsewhere and what exactly the cases were about, I don't know. These matters were referred to the municipal court in Travnik, and I really cannot remember the details of these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you please continue, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware of any soldiers of the 312th Motorised Brigade operating in the area of Guca Gora in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1993, there were no members of the 312th Brigade in the area of Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I asked about June. Perhaps it was a translation error. In June of 1993, were any soldiers of the 312th Motorised Brigade in the area of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither in June of 1993, there were no members of the 312th Motorised Brigade in the area of Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were any members of the 312th Motorised Brigade or any subordinate units of the 312th Motorised Brigade operating in the area of Maline in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were any subordinate units of the 312th Motorised Brigade operating in the area of Cukle or Susanj in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already moved to the area which I'm not familiar with. No, my brigade was not operating in that area, Cukle or Maline. That was the area of another brigade. I did not have any subordinate units of my own that would have been operating in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just to go back to an area we talked a few minutes ago, do you recall or do you have any knowledge of whether any units or subordinate units of the 312th Motorised Brigade were operating in Miletici in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have already indicated as far as that period of time is concerned, which is the subject of your question, the brigade was not operating in that area. That was the area of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Were any subordinate units of the 312th Brigade operating in the area of Ovnak in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were any subordinate units of the 312th Motorised Brigade operating in the area of Brajkovici in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were any subordinate units of the 312th Motorised Brigade operating in the area of Grahovcici in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were any subordinate units of the 312th Motorised Brigade in the area of Vares in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, as the Presiding Judge just mentioned a few moments ago, yesterday you were shown Defence Document 959 which, among other things, indicated that at least up until 2 May 1993, the date of that document, the military police of the 312th had referred several cases of murder to local authorities, or local legal authorities, for action. Do you recall the specifics of any of those cases, those murder cases?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. As far as I remember, there were several cases of traffic violations, even a number of fatalities in these traffic incidents. As for murders, no, I should perhaps have a look at the document. But I really don't remember. I mean, you can -- you know what is contained there. If perhaps documentation from the court could be obtained to that effect, that I would be able to remember. But off the top of my head, no, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the fact that you don't recall, that would include any of the victims or the status of the victims of those alleged murders?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'd like to move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. President, I would ask that the witness be shown one of the videotapes, and I would ask that the sound on that videotape, which is Prosecution Exhibit 762, not be played. In other words, that it just be the video shown to the witness. Before we do that, however, I would like to just explain to the witness exactly what it is we're doing and why it is that we're doing that, if I may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, we're going to show you a videotape which will be visible on the screen in front of you. And I would ask you to take a look at this tape. And during the time that you are viewing the tape, if you recognise the location of where this videotape was made, I would ask you to say so. And you can simply do that as we're watching the tape. I would also ask you if you recognise any person or persons on the videotape, perhaps to indicate by saying "stop" and telling us the name of the person or persons that you might recognise. And finally, at the end of the tape, I will ask you if you're familiar with the contents of what you've seen and if you can any way shed any light on what we've seen on the videotape. Do you understand what I've asked you to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I would ask that Prosecution Exhibit 762 be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the Defence is rising. I think I can anticipate their -- what they want to say. What is the link between the video and the examination-in-chief? Is that what you were going to object to, Ms. Residovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because we do not see any link whatsoever. I should like to see some foundation for this question. Is it the video from the area of responsibility referred to by this witness? That is, the combat lines and the area of responsibility where elements of his brigade were deployed, because after all, that is what he is able to talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two questions: What is the link with other members of the BH Army? They were members of the BH Army after all, so there could possibly be a link. And then the video and the geographical area of his command which was located to the west of Travnik. Mr. Mundis, as far as the Chamber is concerned, if you just tell us 762, it doesn't mean much. Could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask with all due respect if the witness could be escorted out of the courtroom in order for me to respond to these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is exactly what we were going to suggest, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you will have to withdraw for a few moments. Do not stray too far from the courtroom. Mr. Mundis, the witness has left the courtroom so that he cannot be influenced by what you're going to tell us. We're listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, let me put on the record as I should have done also with respect to the last series of questions that of course the Prosecution would assert that this line of questioning as well as the last series of questions on disciplinary issues falls within the scope of Rule 90(H)(ii), and that is that we are required to put our case to witnesses who appear. And that is what we are attempting to do. And although it might under some interpretations fall outside the scope of the direct examination, it is our assertion that Rule 90(H)(ii) requires us to put our case to witnesses, and that is exactly what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You need authorise to do so. In such a case, it is necessary for you to ask the Trial Chamber for authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We will respectfully request that authorisation, Mr. President, and hereby do so. Let me add that tape 762, which is in evidence, the Prosecution believes that this videotape was taken in the town of Travnik. Although there are only a few buildings or other physical features that are visible on the tape because it's primarily people, there are some buildings and locations in the background of that tape which lead us to believe that this witness, as someone who was born and grew up in Travnik, would be able to place this videotape in the town of Travnik. Moreover, we would assert that it goes to the issue of the Muslim forces which the witness talked about yesterday. The videotape has a date stamp on it which the witness may or may not know anything about that time period. If the date stamp is accurate, the witness was certainly in Travnik at the time. There are persons that we believe the witness might be able to identify. As was indicated yesterday I believe at transcript page 41, 42, the witness talked about the Muslim forces or the MS, the Muslimanske Snage, we believe that this videotape might show -- the formation of some of these units. And we believe this videotape was taken in Travnik in August of 1992, which is within the time frame during which the Defence led evidence concerning this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you're requesting leave pursuant to Rule 90(H). We will withdraw for a moments to deliberate. But we will back in a few seconds. But first of all, we will hear what the Defence has to say. The Prosecution was quite clear. This is a videotape that has to do with the town that the witness is very familiar with since he had his office there, he had his headquarters in Travnik. So the Prosecution wants to ask him whether he can recognise his town. So the link is quite evident in that case. And secondly, he wants to ask him whether there are any persons in the video whom he recognises, perhaps his friends. What would you like to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecution correctly quoted 90(H)(i) which says that if a witness can give evidence relevant to the case for the party examining it. However, in (H)(ii) it says, in the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case of the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears, which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness. First of all, my colleague from the Prosecution didn't make that clear to the witness, and in no way did they say there was something in contradiction to the evidence the witness gave. We believe that these arguments should be presented before the Trial Chamber allows us to ask questions -- the witness about the context. This is how we have proceeded. So these questions fall outside the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a point 3 that gives the Trial Chamber discretion to decide on the matter. But as far as item (ii) is concerned, we are being asked whether so far you have elements that contradict what the witness has said in his testimony. So far, he has not denied being in Travnik. He hasn't denied knowing certain people. So in Rule 90 (ii), on the basis of this Rule, is there any information, are there any elements that lead you to believe that the witness might be contradicting himself? Although according to Rule 90(H)(iii), the Trial Chamber has discretion to permit any inquiries. But as far as (H)(ii) is concerned, could you tell us whether you have any elements, any information that might contradict the evidence given by the witness so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps it's an interpretation issue. Our understanding is not that we must demonstrate that the witness has contradicted himself, which is how the English interpretation as reflected in the transcript came from what Your Honour just said. Our interpretation is that it must contradict our case. Our case has been one - and we explained this in our 98 bis submission most recently - that the Travnik -- the Muslim forces in Travnik evolved into the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. This witness yesterday -- and that the TO was involved in that, and eventual evolving nature of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. We explained that in our Rule 98 bis submissions, and if Your Honours would like to me to cite the paragraphs, I can do that. The witness yesterday at pages 41 and 42, and I think again at page 44 if I'm not mistaken, indicated that there were contacts between the commander of the Travnik TO and the Muslim forces in Travnik. He then told us that the Muslim forces did not or were not under the control of the Travnik TO. And I believe that's at line 21 on page 42 of yesterday's transcript. That certainly contradicts the Prosecution case. And we believe that the provisions of Rule 90(H)(i) including the final sentence and Rule 90(H)(ii) permit us to show this to the witness. It's entirely possible he won't recognise anything on the videotape. But we believe that we not only can do this, but the Rules are formulated in such a way that we are required to do that, once again, once we have the Trial Chamber's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will withdraw for a few moments. We have understood the Prosecution has said. The Prosecution says that they have certain elements on the basis of which they believe that what the witness says is in contradiction of the information that they have, and in particular it concerns the Muslim forces present in Travnik. The Prosecution believes there is a contradiction between its case and the testimony of the witness, and this is the reason for which the Prosecution wants to show the witness the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to appeal to you that while determining this issue, perhaps you should have a look at the testimony of the witness. Witness did not mention the 7th Muslim Brigade yesterday. He spoke about the establishment of a group of Muslim forces, as far as I remember. I don't have the relevant line in the transcript, but what the Prosecutor is now trying to tell us, this is not something the witness testified to yesterday. It is not in his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will withdraw, and we will be back in a few seconds. --- Break taken at 4.38 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After having deliberated on the basis of Article 90(H)(iii), the Chamber believes that the Prosecution will be granted leave to ask questions on other -- or additional matters, and in particular, questions on this video about Travnik. Madam Usher, could you call the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Mundis, how long is this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe the excerpt is about 6 to 6 and a half minutes, Mr. President. And again, as with some of the other videos, it's not the best quality, but it's the best we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Caber, you will now be shown a video, and you will tell us what you think about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the person who is speaking now. It's the Mufti from Travnik, Nusret Begovic. He's the one speaking with the loudspeaker now. And the location that we see on the screen, to tell you the truth, I've already seen this clip on our TV in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a political programme which lasted 60 minutes. So I am familiar with some of the scenes. I am not familiar with the part relating to the war, but I have seen the 60-minute long political programme a year or two years ago. That is the only thing I can comment on. But this at the time had nothing to do with me. At the time, I was a member of the Territorial Defence staff in the vicinity of this location, in Medresa, the lower part of Travnik where the headquarters were located some 300 metres away from here. I don't recall that period of time. I was not present when this unit was lined up for inspection, whatever the unit was called. I can only tell you the name that they used in that programme, mujahed. But this is what I learned later on. I don't recall this from the relevant times. The chief of staff had to be present at the front line against the Serbs, and we are talking about the month of August. And what I can tell you about it comes from the fact that I saw the tape and I just recognised the Mufti, Mr. Nusret Begovic, if this is the end of the clip, but there's probably more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There is a little bit more, Mr. President, that we would ask that that also be shown to the witness, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman here is Mr. McLeod [as interpreted]. This one at the left when I arrived in Travnik in 1995, he had his videotheque, a video club from before. These are the people I found when I arrived in Travnik. You told me to identify the people that I know. So that's one of them. Shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could, sir, the name, Mr. McLeod, was that the name of the individual?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mektauf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you spell that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: M-e-k-t-a-u-f.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please indicate to us on the screen, if you still see this individual, which person he is on the screen. And if he's no longer visible, we can rewind the tape a little bit until you again see him.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you rewind a little bit, just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it will take us just a moment to take that clip back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the meantime, sir, do you know the first name or any other information about Mr. Mektauf?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abdul Mektauf, Abdul.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know where he's from?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Either from Iraq or Syria, but I don't know. I really can't remember. I know he's from an Arab country. I knew him because he was in Travnik. I was not interested in him, you know. He lived and worked there, you know. But would you rewind it a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We're still getting that back, sir. I have one last question before we return to the tape. Did Mr. Mektauf speak Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe we've now rewound the tape, and as soon as you see him come on to the screen, if you could tell us to stop, please, and I'll ask you to identify, to describe what he's wearing, what he looks like on the screen that's in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, stop now. Stop. Rewind just a little bit. That's right. The man has his arms behind his back. He's wearing a camouflage T-shirt. He has closely cropped hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is this individual that you're describing clean-shaven or does he have facial hair in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not very clear. I don't think he's clean-shaven. Perhaps he has a two- or three-day beard, but he's wearing a camouflage T-shirt. His arms are behind his back, and if we're looking at the same image, it says LP on his belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would just simply for the sake of continuity, Mr. President, ask that the videotape be played to its end, and then I'll have a few remaining questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, if you spot anyone else or any other identifying feature on this tape, tell us to stop the tape and we'll again stop the tape. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, just to clarify then, the only two individuals that you recognised were Mr. Begovic and Mr. Mektauf. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdibegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please again for the transcript spell that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A-v-d-i-b-e-g-o-v-i-c. Avdibegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Witness, can you tell us the location of where that videotape was taken, if you know.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see that this was shot in front of the Medresa in Travnik. That's at the entrance to Travnik. It's as you approach Travnik from the eastern direction, from the direction of Vitez towards Jajce, or rather Turbe. Do you know what a Medresa is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could explain that for the benefit of everyone in and around the courtroom, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the Medresa was used as a furniture salon. During the communist period, it was a furniture salon. But a long time ago, at the time of the Osmanlije, it was a religious school, a secondary religious school for pupils of Islamic faith. That's what a Medresa is. This name has been maintained because of the -- for traditional reasons, because of the cultural situation. Because Travnik was the centre of the Osmanlije Kingdom for a certain period of time, in the 15th and 16th century. That is why the Medresa has that name, and it has its own traditions, and it has a certain history. But when this video was shot, it was used as a furniture salon. It was used as a furniture salon at the time of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us yesterday about the Muslim forces or the Muslimanske Snage or MS, that was formed in Travnik. Do you remember telling us about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. At the time of the TO staff, the time of the detachment and the regional staffs, yes, I remember this. In the area of the municipality, in the centre of town, someone launched the initiative to form Muslim forces. They were supposed to follow a certain code of conduct, et cetera. And these forces were not under the command of the TO staff. And they went into action in the direction of the Serbian forces in the area of Vlasic, in the area near to Jajce and at the time that Karaula was in the hands of the TO. And later, they were in the Bjelo Buca area. And once the army and brigades had been formed, sometime in November, a battalion was formed out of these Muslim forces, the 7th Muslim Battalion, and its headquarters were in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So sir, you're telling us that the Muslim forces from Travnik later became the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they became part of the 7th Muslim Brigade. A battalion was formed. They became a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: They became part of the 1st Battalion of the 7th. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that was the battalion which remained in Travnik through 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether they were there all the time, but yes, it was -- its location was linked to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir -- you told us that -- I believe you just said someone was involved in forming the Muslim forces. Do you know who? Who were the leaders? Who were the people involved in establishing the Muslim forces in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Whatever I said, it would only be guesswork. And it would be based on newspaper reports, et cetera. If I go back to that time, I can claim that I didn't know who the people who initiated this were. But let me tell you that at that time, when I go back to that period, to the year 1992 and 1993, or rather 1992 when the Muslim forces were in that area, this didn't bother us, the TO staff, because they were obedient. They carried out orders, but they weren't under our command. They followed to an extent, or they followed more or less the code of conduct for members of the Islam faith. They followed a code of conduct that perhaps wasn't exactly the same of that of other units or that of the TO. But as to who was responsible for its formation, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know Asim Koricic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Asim Koricic. I saw him at that time in 1992 and in 1993, too. He is someone who often appeared in the TO staff. He would have coffee there, speak to the commander. They probably spoke about other matters, too. At the time, I think he was a commander. I'm not a hundred per cent sure, but I think he was the commander of those forces at that time because according to the chronology, later there was the brigade formation, then the commander of brigades, and commanders of battalions, et cetera. But I'm not familiar with all of this. I don't want to get involved in guesswork.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us yesterday at page 42, line 21 of the transcript that there were contacts between the commander of the Travnik TO and the MS or Muslimanske Snage, Muslim forces in Travnik. What type of contacts were these?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very frequently, the staff commander didn't have the duty of informing his staff about his conversations with his colleague, with another commander. I assume that there could only have been a form of cooperation in terms of engaging forces, where such forces were not sufficient, in areas where they were fighting Serbian areas. That this was the area that the TO staff covered, from Vlasic then up to Turbe, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: /Sir, the Muslim forces or MS in Travnik, was that unit or organ or organisation comprised of local Bosnians or foreigners or both?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's interesting to note that at that time in Travnik, people from Arab countries also started appearing, just like members of humanitarian organisations and journalists came. They came to see and to film what was happening to the Bosniak people. And I remember that in 1992, there were a lot of Arabs who, in the presence of the president of the municipality, came to offer assistance to the TO and to the refugees. They wanted to offer humanitarian assistance and food, but they also wanted to help TO units that had logistical problems. As far as the Muslim forces are concerned, as far as I can remember, they mostly consisted of Bosniaks, Bosniaks from that area, you know. I know that later on, quite a few people came from Bosanska Krajina. There were young men who became part of that formation. And they followed this code of conduct. I know that at that time, before the formation of the brigade, before the formation of the 7th Brigade, or rather, before the formation of the battalion for Travnik, there were some of those people, there were some of those Arabs who were part of these forces. As to what they did exactly, well, it was probably what I was saying yesterday. It probably had to do with the Croatian people and all those who wanted to help the Croatian people -- well I assume they wanted to help the Muslim people, just like others wanted to help the Croatian people. I saw two or three people in uniform who were members of the Muslim forces at that time; that is to say, before the formation of the 7th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say you saw people in uniform who were members of the Muslim forces at that time, were you referring to foreigners?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were probably foreigners. They were certainly foreigners. They weren't people whom I knew from Travnik; therefore, they were foreigners. I pointed to a man who was a foreigner at one point in time, but then he became a Bosniak national. But as far as these other people are concerned at the time, they were foreigners, at least as far as I was concerned. I was an onlooker from the side. As to whether they had any valid, legitimate documents, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And sir, when you say "I pointed to a man who was a foreigner at that point in time," you're referring to Mr. Mektauf?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think he was a foreigner at that time. He was a member of the Bosniak people. I believe that he had the documents at the time according to which he was a Bosnian. Because when I went to Travnik, I lived in Travnik. I know that he had a shop of his own, a video club, and I don't believe that as a foreigner he could have received permission to have a private business of his own if he had not been a national of Bosnia. I don't think that at that time in 1992 he was a foreigner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But you told us he was not born in Bosnia. I believe you said Syria or Iraq.

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. He wasn't born in Bosnia. As I said, he came earlier on. According to the information I heard, all citizens in Travnik knew this gentleman. Travnik is a small town. Everyone knows that there was a video club called Palma, and that's where people would go to borrow videos before the war. I don't know what else I could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that there were foreigners who came and also a number of humanitarian agencies and a number of refugees. There were a large number of people who were not from Travnik who came to Travnik in 1992. Is that an accurate summation?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any idea as to an approximate number of foreign, middle-eastern individuals who came to the Travnik area and who became soldiers or fighters in the Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: ZIJAD CABER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really don't have a precise idea. It would just be guesswork. As I said, two or three men, a while ago. There were a few of them in town. There were a few uniformed individuals from Arab countries, as you say, or from the near east. You know, I'm trying to be frank. I could tell you about something that I saw later on, but I'm trying to be frank and tell you about 1992, about what I saw in 1992. I didn't see many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
